proof: Emulators recreate a console so they can run its library. Retro Porting Toolkit recompiles one game at a time instead, keeping the original game logic and replacing the hardware constraints around it. Less breadth, far more control over rendering, input, networking, and behavior.
Correctness is measured against the emulator cores the community already trusts. Seven PlayStation games are playable today. The Virtual Boy has one, and vbrecomp still calls itself a tech demo.
philosophy: Go native. Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, even the browser. No emulator core in sight.
See more of the world. Adaptive widescreen up to 21:9 in games like Tomba! 2 and Mega Man Zero.
Break the old limits. 60 FPS patches, CD-quality MSU-1 soundtracks, voxel 3D remixes, and mod loaders that never touch your original ROM.
Swap the hardware. Spin WarioWare: Twisted! with your phone or a DualSense, and let real local weather drive Boktai's solar sensor.
Change the words. Runtime text replacement powers Tsumu Light's English fan translation and NES text overrides.
Play together. Shared netplay, rollback, save states, and rewind (recomp-net and retcomm-rbengine) that every ecosystem can pick up.
constraintsIntro: Features layer over your own copy while the game runs, rather than patching it. Turn one off and the original comes back.

stories.title: The map was already loaded. The screen was hiding it.
stories.body: Game Boy Advance games often load much of their map and overworld into memory at once, and the size of the screen was the only thing keeping it out of sight. Mega Man Zero opens the logical view past the original 240 pixels, 288 recommended and the wider settings still validation targets, so a threat is on screen before it is on top of you. Enemies keep their original spawn rules, so things can still appear near the new edges.
stories.alt: Mega Man Zero running with the view opened past the original Game Boy Advance width

stories.title: Boktai still runs on sunlight. Yours.
stories.body: The cartridge carried a real light sensor: the solar gun charged from actual sunlight, and the undead could only be sealed while you had light. A community build keeps the requirement and moves the sensor. Give it a postal code and the weather where you are drives the gauge, empty at night, a bar or three under heavy cloud, full in clear midday, with the full sun point adjustable. Give it no postal code and nothing ever leaves your machine.
stories.alt: Boktai running with its solar gauge driven by local weather

stories.title: The words can change while the game runs.
stories.body: Faxanadu is the showcase for the NES framework's text override: dialogue and glyphs are replaced at runtime from a data file, with hot reload, so an edit shows up in the running game about a second later. The same idea carries a whole game on PlayStation, where Tsumu Light, a puzzle game that never left Japan, now reads in English without the disc being touched.
stories.alt: Faxanadu running as a native PC application

platformNote.title: Each console teaches the next.
platformNote.body: The DS recompiler's second processor began as the Game Boy Advance one. The CD-i's 68000 front end came out of the Genesis work.
